utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present the. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Krgovic, and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution is composition team as yesterday, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Witness is already present. We finished the cross-examination yesterday. Mr. Bourgon, you had indicated you have redirect. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't have too many questions for you this morning, but immediately I will ask my colleague from the Prosecution to hand over to you the original of Exhibit P354, which is the attendance roster for the Military Police Company of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can have it in e-court at the same time, please. That's P354, and I'd like the last page of this document which is 6615.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at the last page of this document, I think it's on the reverse side on 6615, where you have some abbreviations that you included on this document. You see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 54, line 17 to 20, my colleague asked you about the abbreviation "BO" used in the MP attendance roster for July. And you stated that this referred to persons on sick leave, and you also used the example of Dragan Asceric at line 79. My question is the following: To your knowledge, the military policemen who were sent to Orahovac that night, were they fit for combat? In other words, were they injured in any way or sick in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were fit. None of them were either sick or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, had these military policemen that night before Jasikovac arrived, had they received any order to remain at Standard, or did they just happen to be there because their work day was over or their duties were over for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just some clarification as to when we are talking about for this question. There's no time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, I'm sure will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My questions refer to that night and that night, I thought that was clear, that this referred to the night they went to Orahovac, but I will make my questions more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, the night that the military policemen were sent to Orahovac by Jasikovac, according to your testimony, before Jasikovac arrived, had the military policemen received any order to remain at Standard, or did they just happen to be there because their work day was over?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was carrying out their duties at Standard, they all had their daily assignments, and that is why they remained at Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Looking at the attendance roster that is before you, can you tell me if the name of Drago Nikolic appears on this roster.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell me why this is so?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic was not a member of the Military Police Company. He was not on our register.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about the name of your commander Jasikovac, does it appear on the roster; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, under number 1, as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At page 65 of the transcript yesterday, lines 4 to 6, you stated the following: "I would not have liked to have gone anyway because in Baljkovica, you could see for yourself the list how many wounded and how many were killed, including my brother Dragan." Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother Aco, not Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, also at page 60, lines 9 to 12, the following questions was put to you by my colleague, and he was then quoting from the transcript of your January 2006 interview. So what I'm about to read is something that was in your interview. My colleague said, page 65: "And the question was put to you: 'How do you know people were not willing to go?' "And your answer was: 'One could see. One could see on their faces; and for me, it was an extremely great pleasure to hear that I should not go.'" Based on this answer, my question is the following: the fact that you could see on the faces of the MPs that they were not willing to go in Orahovac, did that have anything to do with the executions that we now know later took place in that area.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody knew about the executions quite simply. People would have preferred not to have gone. The very thought of guarding prisoners; and as far as the executions were concerned, I don't think that they knew anything about this, and that applies to all military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, the fact that you, as you mentioned, that it was an extremely great pleasure to hear that you would not go, did that have anything to do with the executions that we now know happened later in this area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, to the best of your recollection, were the members of the Military Police Company ever glad and eager to go in the field where combat was taking place or combat could take place?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody wants to or likes to go where there was shooting. If they had to go, they did go, but not because they wished to do so, because lots of people died in the shootings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, the military policemen who were sent to Orahovac, to your knowledge, were they told anything other than the fact that they were going to secure prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Jasikovac had told us that we were going to guard the POWs, and that's all. Nothing else was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at page 58, lines 5 to 7, my colleague asked you this question about the lawyer Cedo Jovic, and I quote: "When they returned from Orahovac, one of them told you that they no longer had their rifles. Do you remember that?" Your answer, confirming that they no longer had their rifles with them and that they told you, is at page 58, lines 8 to 11. My question today is the following: Did -- when you had this conversation with Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic, did they mention to you that their weapons had been taken away by members of the army who were not from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what they told me about who had taken their weapons. All I know is that they came and said that they had their rifles no longer with them and that somebody had taken them from them. I don't know who that somebody was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at page 58, lines 14, right up to page -- it's 68, sorry, 68, lines 14 to 76, lines 29, my colleague went on to quote some questions and answers from your interview, but he missed some lines that I would like to read to you. So I will now read to you your interview, and I will start at page 75, line 14. Line 14 reads as follows: "Did you speak with Cedo and Bogdanovic? What was going on in Orahovac? " Your answer was: "They don't like to speak about it." Then my colleague missed a part where you said: "They did not comment anything about it simply ..." -- sorry: "They did comment anything about it simply." Then at lines 21: "Did you hear what happened in Orahovac?" Your answer: "Everybody knows. Everybody knows that they executed these people there. Investigator: "Okay." Your answer: "That's not an issue." Investigator: "When did you find out that people were executed there?" The Interpreter asked: "When?" And your answer was: "After the execution, after that." Investigator asked you: "How long after that." And your answer was: "I don't know. Probably that same evening. That was then said, but I don't know who said it." The investigator went on to ask you, but my colleague did not quote this part of your interview: "But when did people came back from Orahovac? They were speaking about what happened over there, how it happened." And you said: "Which people, our people? " The investigator said: "Yeah, I mean the military police." Your answer, always on the part that is not quoted by my colleague: "I don't know, really. Believe me, I don't know. I didn't like to comment it at all, and I didn't like to talk about it." The investigator went on to say: "Yes, I understand. But you said that you learned that the people were executed the same day." And your answer was: "Yes, but I don't know how and who did it, and they didn't talk about it." Based on what I just read to you from your interview, do you stand by what you said back then completed as I just read it to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, so the record is clear, if -- and we can, I think, deal with this one of two ways, either at the tendering time offer this entire section of the interview so that the Court can see exactly how the questioning went. Otherwise, I'd ask my friend to continue reading the question and answer so that the Court can see where it overlaps with the very questions that I asked the witness. Otherwise, the Court will not have a fair view of how this series of questions went, since my friend is not putting the pages or so forth and the lines. But I think the Court should see the entire set of questions and how my questioning and the questioning that my friend is putting to the witness mesh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague had the opportunity to read all the questions during his cross-examination, and I'm taking this opportunity to make corrections and I'm indicating where in the interview there were thing that is were missed. In any event, if my colleague wants to ask for the interview of the witness to be included in the record for impeachment purposes, then I will have no objections to that, because he asked so many questions about. I think it will be interesting for the Judges to see exactly everything the witness said during his interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough. Let's proceed and we'll determine this issue later on. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, what I read this morning, does that correspond to what you remember telling the Prosecution at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is: To the best of your recollection, when is the first time you heard information or rumours about executions taking place in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the following day, but I really have no idea when I heard about it. I think it was the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague went on to ask you a very long question, which can be found in the transcript at page 76 starting at line 16, until page 79 at line 6, so about a three-page question. And when he asked this question to you, he quoted from your interview, and he read bits and pieces from pages 54, 55, 78, 84, 86, and 89. My question to you is the following to try to make the record clear: To the best of your recollection, did you know at the time that the Military Police Company went to Rocevic on 15 July as suggested by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know at all that they were at Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall using, when writing this attendance roster that you have before you, using the letter "R" for Romeo?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we go back to the last page of this document at the end, where you did include some abbreviations, was the letter "R" ever included in this list of abbreviations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first page of this document that you have before you, on the top should read "6610," my colleague draw your attention to the columns of the 14th and the 15th; and he asked you whether you had made a whole bunch of changes to the column of the 14th and to the column of the 15th. My question is: If there are changes in these columns, as you testified about, did you make other changes to this form throughout the month of July?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For example, if we look at line 12, we see a bunch of Ts that seem to be -- or to have been written over crosses in a number of places. Are these change that is you made to this form?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we would look at other records or other attendance records for other months for the Military Police Company, would we also see some change that you made regularly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Often, when it was necessary or when there were any changes to daily orders, if there was any action to be carried out, people would be re-assigned to the field. This probably happened during other months as well, but I don't have these papers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you were questioned about Orahovac by the investigators back in 2006, in your interview you mentioned some names that you did remember were sent to Orahovac that night. Do you remember the names that you knew immediately when the questions was put to you that had been to Orahovac that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I remember Commander Jasikovac having left, as well as Nada Stojanovic, Cedo Jovic, and Goran Bogdanovic. I can remember those four people and not any others. After the investigator showed me the roster for the MP company, then I realized that there were some other people who had left as well, and they were mentioned yesterday by the Prosecutor. But even as I speak here today, I still don't remember them having left, but their names appear on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, the four names that you did mention at the beginning, for example, you said Bogdanovic and Jovic, were these persons friends of yours at the time, or how close were you to these people?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was close with them then and now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you have any hesitation to tell the investigators that you remembered these people going to Orahovac on that night, despite the fact that they are your friends?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember them first, and I couldn't remember the rest. I mentioned a few of my best friends that were up there, proving that I wasn't trying to cover up for anyone who is in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, between July 1995, between exactly those events and today, did you hear any rumours that Jasikovac and some military policemen from the company actually went to Rocevic? Did you hear any rumours about that since July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I didn't discuss Rocevic with anyone; and even today, I don't know whether they were there or not. As I said yesterday, they may have left Orahovac to go to Rocevic, but I wasn't notified and I wasn't told by anyone later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you hear stories about that, that you could not confirm?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, on page 83, my colleague made reference to page 7 of your interview; and on that interview, on that page, you said that the military company had a warehouse where you kept ammunition and weapons and that you were in charge of that. So I will quote what you said yesterday, at lines 10 to 16 of page 83. Answer: "When the military policemen went to Orahovac, they had their rifles. Each policemen had been issued with an automatic rifle and each rifle had its serial number. They had rifles and ammunition. We did not issue any additional ammo at that time. If needed, it was myself who went to the logistics department to take ammunition, if we needed it, for the unit. The same goes for any food. I would take those and issue them to the soldiers." Sir, based on what you stated, at lines 10 to 16, I would like to know, if you recall of course, when the military policemen went to Orahovac, did you issue them ammunition in addition to what each member normally carried with his weapon?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you issue any additional ammunition to the Military Police Company in Orahovac during the next 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not issue any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you receive a request to send food to Orahovac, or did you send actually food to Orahovac during the next 24 hours for the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust me when I say that I don't remember whether I had some food issued to me so that I could pass it on. I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 83, lines 16 to 18, that's just the part that follows, you stated that whether or not food was issued or requested for the prisoners of war, you don't know because this was not part of your duties. Sorry. I'm reading my question now and not from the transcript. So to avoid any objection, I will read exactly what you said. Lines 16 to 18 and that is page 83: "As for the food for the prisoners, I have no idea about that. I could not be issued any food for prisoners. I could only receive food for the MP members." Now, my question was: If there was or was not food issued to the prisoners or arrangements made for them to have food, would you be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not have probably because it was the logistics that delivered food. I have no idea whether I would have been notified or not. If they did issue some food, they probably would have sent that on some trucks to Orahovac; therefore, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on page 84, lines 3 to 6, my colleague raised the issue of dates, and he suggested that you cannot tell what were the exact dates of the days you testified about with precision. So I have a few questions regarding dates. The first one being: Do you remember the day that you saw the buses driving in front of Standard with the prisoners, as you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you remember how many days you saw buses going in front of Standard with prisoners? Only one day or more than one day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only one day that I saw them passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that it is the night before that you saw the buses that the MPs went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the day when the buses passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that night that you were assigned on duty at the Karakaj bridge, is that the same night that you went -- that the MPs went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next day you remember that it's the next day that you relieved by Bovo Nikovic, as you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've let it slide, but we are really leading, and it's asked and answered on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Mr. President. I think that it's important for the witness to put the events in sequence, so that he knows about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's an intermediate question leading to another, okay, go ahead; but please try to avoid being repetitive either on your side or on the witness's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is direct, of course. I mean, it's a very leading question, but I take it that it's an intermediate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The day that -- you testified yesterday, sir, that both you and Jeremic were at Standard. This is the same day that you saw the buses -- or is it the same day that you saw the buses with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the buses on that one day. There were no other days that the buses were passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is that the day that you were alone with Jeremic in Standard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, we went over this in the direct examination, my friend went through a very careful sequence of events, and now he is leading the witness repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, I'm leading, but it's a result of the cross-examination where he tried to mix the witness up with the events. So I'm certainly allowed to ask the witness whether the day he saw the buses is the day that he was alone with Jeremic at Standard. There's absolutely nothing wrong with that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. I asked this witness one question on that issue because it was clear to me that there were no dates elicited on purpose during direct. I did not go through any sequence of events with this witness, so the insinuation there's any mixing up is erroneous. And my friend cannot try to lead this witness on what are not intermediate issues, but the very issues he is trying to establish. It's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We've discussed this amongst ourselves and the conclusion we arrive at is that, like before, we consider this both leading -- both leading and a question that has been asked and answered already. But unlike previously, this time we are not going to allow it. So let's proceed. If you want to go straight to where you are heading, go straight there, Mr. Bourgon. I mean, avoid the roundabout, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the roster in front of you and if you look at the dates -- can you look at the attendance roster before you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What night were the military police sent to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By looking at the register in front of you, that's the attendance log, my questions -- my colleague put questions to you yesterday about changes being made. Can you tell us what is the date of the night that the military policemen were sent to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Does that correspond to the day they were there or to the night that they were sent?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was that day that they were sent to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, one last question I have for you concerning a question that was put to you by my colleague: Did you see any unknown civilian walking in Standard Barracks between the gate and the command building on the day you were there with Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've two very brief questions that arise directly from the redirect, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can the witness remove his headphones first, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can allow him to hear, if you want. But anyway, remove them. It's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't know if he is still psychic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two very brief issues. One is my friend, in trying to clarify the issue with respect to these two lawyers, asked a question that was outside of the area that I was putting that question with respect to the two lawyers for, and I'd just like to address complete the answer that this witness gave in his interview so that we can put that in the appropriate context. It's simply to ask the witness to confirm something he said in this paragraph. It's one page, page 75 of his interview. With respect, my friend asked him a question about who these soldiers were that took the weapons away from Bogdanovic and Jovic, and what he said was that they were not members of the Zvornik Brigade. That is not something I was interested in dealing with; but now that it's arisen, I think it's fair to complete what this witness said, which is: "I think when they were about to be dismissed from the unit that they returned their weapons." That's all I want to ask the witness to confirm, that one answer that he gave, and I think that fairly arises from the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The other question has to do with my friend asked this witness about the four MPs that he has said are his close friends and why it was that he very willingly recalled their named. Again, as part of that answer, there's one line that I want to ask him whether he can confirm giving that answer. It is at line 25, page 66 of his interview, where he says: "I think Dragan Jovanovic, he went." Then he says: "I know that Nikolic, Drago's brother, went." And I just want to find out why it is or whether this individual is somebody in the same category that my friend elicited on redirect somebody that was his friend and whether that's why he know that is this person went or if there's another reason why this he knows that this person went. I think that fairly arises from the thrust of the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I object to both questions, Mr. President. My colleague had every opportunity to ask questions about the interview, and the issues that are raised are not related to what my colleague would like to attempt to do at this point in time. The witness, when he answered my question this morning, said: "I remember those names. "He gave four names. He said: "The others I remember after I saw what the duty roster was given to me." That was very clear. What the witness answered today was very clear, and the Judges will probably most likely have the interview and they can make their own mind as professional judges in terms of seeing if there was anything that was -- that should be asked to the witness. The other question about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The first question that my colleague said, once again the answer from the witness was very clear. I would have liked him to say something that he said elsewhere that those people were not from the Zvornik Brigade, but he did not say that. So I think we can leave it at that, Mr. President, and we are just wasting time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision, you see we reach our decisions quite fast and unanimously as well. Our decision is not to allow the questions. Main reason, apart from what was stated by Mr. Bourgon, is that we are going to have the document in any case. Plus, the statement of what our attention should be drawn at has already been stated by Mr. Thayer, so there is no need to put the questions. Mr. Kostic, we've come to the end of your journey here. No more questions for you, which means you can leave this courtroom and go back home. You will receive all the assistance you need from our staff. But before you leave the courtroom, I wish to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having come over, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Documents? Mr. Bourgon, I have three -- five documents indicated here, and that includes the ones he has marked during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All we have, Mr. President, is the pictures that were marked in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I have the numbers of these documents that were given to me, but we lost the small yellow paper with the IC numbers that were given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry. I have them. If you want to check, it's 3D497, and then IC 3D218, IC 3D219, 220, and 221. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Those are, in fact, the IC numbers, Mr. President. I thank you for your assistance. I lost my small paper here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you object to any of these documents, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone else for that matter? No objections. They are admitted. Do you have any documents, no, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President, just three. I think everything else that we used is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interview, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have the interview, that is 3754; the logistics company attendance roster for July '95, that's 3726; I believe the engineering roster is already in; and then we have the 1st Battalion signal squad attendance roster for July 1995, that's 3760.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is something wrong in the transcript at line 25 of page 19. It says I object the engineering roster, but anyway that object is out of place. Any objection, Mr. Bourgon, to these three documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President, other than the fact that I know for the record that all these attendance logs, they should have been in the Prosecution from the get-go. The fact that they bring these witnesses here at this time is completely contrary to the spirit and the object of the rule 65 ter. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections from anyone else? These documents are admitted. Let's continue with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to note, Mr. President, in the transcript, it says Mr. Ostojic is speaking, and I would not want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I suggest you avoid that sort of confusion as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With the size, it shouldn't be too difficult, but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this one 3DW-17, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 16, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 16. Okay. Remind me when we come to number 17 that I need to tell you something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, sir. You are Mr. Jeremic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. You are most welcome. I see that you have some legal background which makes it is easier for you and for us, and for everybody for that matter. Before you start giving evidence, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text is going to be given to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable, take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You have been here before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you know the procedure. This time it's Mr. Bourgon who - is it Mr. Bourgon or Ms. Nikolic - Mr. Bourgon who will be putting to you questions first. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon; and along with my colleagues, Ms. Jelena Nikolic and Ms. Marie-Claude Fournie, we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Before we begin, I would just like to remind you that if there is a question that you do not understand, please do not hesitate in asking me to say that question over again, so that we are clear as to what is being asked. Sir, can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you testified before this Tribunal as a witness for the Prosecution on 24 and 25 April 2007. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you testified before, I only have a few questions for you today, which deals specifically with the day that you were on duty at the gate in front of Standard barracks. My first question is: Do you remember testifying about the time you were on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to put a few questions to you which were not put to you at the time, and I will begin with the following: To the best of your recollection, when did your period of duty at the gate begin? When is it that you were first told that you would be on duty?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As I said last time, I can't recall the exact date, but I do know that it was after Srebrenica had fallen. I don't know whether it was the 13th or 14th of July. I can't say that with any degree of certainty, but it was after Srebrenica had fallen; therefore, in mid-July, the 13th, the 14th, the 15th perhaps. I'm not sure about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone to his right or closer to the one to his left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The witness said something. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we didn't receive interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you add something to your answer?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I said that I definitely remember being at the gate, and that that was after the fall of Srebrenica, whether it was the 14th, the 13th, but that period anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you remember that in your testimony you mentioned that you saw buses driving in front of Standard Barracks with prisoners in them? Do you recall testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I testified to these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And taking this day with the buses as a reference point, when did your period of duty at the gate begin?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, as I just said, I cannot give you the exact date when I was there, but I was there. I started my duty shift in the afternoon; but whether it was on the afternoon of the 13th or the 14th, I don't know. I was at the gate for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, of course, I'm not looking for an exact date. I'm just looking the day you saw the buses, did your duty begin that day or did your duty begin another day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It was on the previous day that I was at the gate, the previous day, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who assigned you to be on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The MP company commander, Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that a regular tour of duty for you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, that was an emergency. I very seldom was posted at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall what the -- what was happening that -- or the reasons for which you had to be put on duty on that date?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was happening?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, all the MPs were away in the field. I don't know exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall -- you mentioned earlier on that you were on duty for 24 hours. Do you recall who replaced you at the end of this 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Another military policemen replaced me, but I don't remember his name. I know that as soon as they returned from the field, one of the MPs replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, were you alone on duty that day at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, as an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where exactly is the military policeman working from when he is on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, he is at the gate to the Standard Barracks, quite close to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would now like, sir, to show you a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I could have in e-court, please, 3D497.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to look at this picture, and my first question is: Do you recognise the picture? This will appear in front of you. Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe what it is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what we called the reception area. That's the entrance to the Standard barracks in Zvornik; and, normally, but not normally, this is where the MPs were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe what is inside that room?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, I can describe it. On the right-hand side, there was a room where usually a policeman was sitting, there was a telephone there as well, and another policeman was usually standing outside of the reception area. Normally, there were two men to the shift; but when I was on duty, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness was referring to Exhibit 3D497. And if I can now have in e-court, 3D500, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I will show you a new picture, and I would like you to tell us if you recognise this picture. Do you recognise the picture?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: This is the gate, an entrance gate to standard. It's a sliding gate, and it's purpose was to serve as a door. And on the left-hand side, I can see a part that served as a barrier that was raised when vehicles entered or exited the compound of Standard. This was a big gate, and this is the gate through which vehicles entered the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. With the assistance of the court usher, I will ask you to make a marking on this picture. You will be given a pen which actually allows you to mark something on the screen in front of you, and I would simply like you to draw a circle where you say there was this, I think you used the words, "barrier that was raised when vehicles entered or exited the compound of Standard." Can you put a circle around that with the pen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I remember. This is this part here. This barrier is not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The first gate that you said was a sliding gate, can you also put a circle around that, if you see that sliding gate on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak into his microphone to the right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see it. This is this big gate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I can just ask you at the bottom of this picture to put your initials and today's date, which is 23 September 2008, at the bottom of this picture.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We won't be needing that, so if we can save this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what was the role of the military policeman on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, the role of the military policeman was as follows: To check both civilian and military vehicles coming in. The military vehicles were passed through by having the barrier raised, and civilian vehicles were also checked, as well as civilians were. They would enter through a smaller gate, the one that you cannot see in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you check all vehicles and persons coming into Standard Barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did not check military vehicles at that time, and I knew a lot of members of the Zvornik Brigade, so there was no need for me to check on them. I knew that those were our military vehicles, so I didn't halt them. I just raised the barrier and let them pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about civilian vehicles, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, as for civilian vehicles, they were not allowed to enter the Standard Barracks. I would stop them, and they were allowed to park the vehicles behind this fence. There was a parking area there, and that is where they will leave their vehicles. They were not allowed to enter the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What about a civilian vehicle that was either driven by or there was a passenger who was a member of the brigade? To use a very easy example, what about if the commander of the brigade came in, in a vehicle that looked civilian, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, I would allow the commander to get in. I would raise the barrier and allow him entrance. I would not check on him because I knew who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at what point would you determine whether you would stop or not the vehicle when it was a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this : This gate that I see in front of me was only halfway open and the other half was blocked by the barrier. As I would approach the barrier, I would look into the vehicle and act accordingly. If it was the military vehicle, I would let it pass through. If it was a civilian vehicle, I would not let them in, but, rather, direct them to the nearby parking-lot. You can see that right behind this fence, there's a vehicle parked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what was the normal procedure once you turned back a civilian vehicle? What would that person do then?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: If they wanted to enter the barracks, he would come to me, introduce himself, to say what the purpose of his visit was, and where he wanted to go. I would check their ID to verify their identity; and depending on who they wished to see, I would act accordingly. If this person was going to the command HQ, I would advise the duty operations officer; and if it was, if I may say, a visitor of minor importance looking for a soldier, I would call this soldier by telephone and ask him to come over to the gate and to have their conversation there. That was the usual procedure. If anyone wanted to go to see the commander or any other high ranking officer at the command HQ, I would notify the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you let at any time an unknown civilian walk in the barracks without an escort?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Civilians were not allowed to enter the barracks, unknown civilians. In general, civilians had to give their notice of the visit and to leave all their personal details with the military policeman at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened to the civilian after he had checked in with the military police on duty at the gate? What would happen then?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As I said, depending on who, where they wanted to go, if they were going to the command building, then military policemen would escort him to the point where he wished to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I now turn to the morning when you were on duty at the gate. My first question is the following: Do you remember which members of the Military Police Company were present at Standard on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: When I was at the gate, I don't think that there were any members of the MP company there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, in your testimony, you said that you did not remember, and I quote from page 10445, for my colleague, you said that you "... did not remember seeing any officers who were not from the Zvornik Brigade coming in or going out from Standard Barracks during that day; although, this is possible." Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I didn't know any other officers other than those from the Zvornik Brigade. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about civilians, do you recall seeing any civilians arriving at Standard Barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Go on, sir. I did not want to interrupt you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, all I wanted to say to that was that an emergency situation and there were very few civilians even on the streets, let alone having them come to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If two civilians dressed in civilian and driving a civilian car had arrived at Standard on that day, would you have seen them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were there any other entrances to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in July 1995, did you know who Ratko Vidovic was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you have recognised him in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, in July 1995, did you know who Vojislav Jekic was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I had heard of him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And could you have recognised Vojislav Jekic in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if either or both of these individuals would have arrive at Standard on that day, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I would deny them entry to Standard. I would have to note down their details, personal details, and ask them where they were going. So their identity had definitely had to be established. I would stop them at the gate and tell them, "Gentlemen, you have to state your name -- names and show me your documents and tell me where you were heading."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall calling the duty officer on that day to announce the arrival of any visitors or civilian visitors that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember calling the operations duty officer or the duty officer in order to announce the arrival of civilians unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, were there many vehicles coming in or going out of Standard barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, the usual. Maybe a slightly higher number than on any other day, but I didn't count the vehicles, and I really cannot give you an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you see Drago Nikolic arrive at Standard Barracks during that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember really seeing Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, after that day that you were on duty at Standard Barracks, what did you do in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, I was replaced by a military policemen who had come back from the field and I resumed my normal duties afterwards, the duties that I discharged at the MP company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, how many times did you meet with members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic since your testimony in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: With the Defence team? Well, they would come to Zvornik, I think, on two or three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with me in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. You came as well. We had coffee together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many times, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Twice. I think twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you meet with our investigator Radovan Keslelj?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my colleague just reminded me I missed a question. Do you remember meeting with me in The Hague during the past few days?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did anyone from the Defence team of Drago Nikolic ask you to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No. You didn't ask me to sign any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember what kind of questions either myself or the investigator put to you when we met in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, the questions referred to whether I knew Jekic or Vidovic, and whether they had come to the Standard Barracks while I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you asked any questions about the procedure for the military police on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It might have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic try to influence your testimony in any way?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have one last question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to come back to the picture, the first one that we used today, which is 3D497. If we can have this in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony today, that's on page 26 -- 27, lines 1 to 3, talking about civilians, you mentioned: "They would enter through a smaller gate, the one that you cannot see in this picture." Now, my question is: Do you see this smaller gate that you were talking about in this picture.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the big gate was used to let vehicles pass through and the smaller gate was for pedestrians, and you can see it here next or leaning to the reception area or this duty booth or the reception area, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe if I can ask the court usher, to be on the safe side, so I would ask you to identify with this pen with this gate where civilians used to come, so if you can make a circle around that gate.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That's the one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one further question: To the left of this picture, we see a building in the back. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That's the Standard Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you can sign this picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sign it and date it, and we'll break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see the date on it. Okay. We'll have a 25 minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you think your cross-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We estimated 30 minutes, Mr. President. I think I should be able to stay within that estimate. I may need a couple of minutes on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we don't have any other witnesses after that today; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President. The next witness is ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay, okay. I thought the next witness was the videolink one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Both videolink witnesses are tomorrow, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again, to you, sir. It's nice to see you again. We have to stop meeting like this. How many times --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I hope so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How many times -- well, you testified that you met with the Defence two or three times before coming to The Hague. Were you shown any documents during any of your meetings, or were you given any information to help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't try to suggest anything. I don't know. I don't think they showed me any documents. Well, I've already explained what were the circumstances that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. So your recollection is -- or your testimony is based solely on your recollection of these events; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that the specific names that stick out in your mind about whom the Defence was interested when they met with you were that of Vojislav Jekic and Ratko Vidovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of anyone else who the Defence asked you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. We spoke mostly about Vidovic and Jekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you recall obviously testifying here on the 24th and 25th of April 2007, and you also testified in the Trbic trial in Sarajevo on 19 December 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you testified in this case, my colleague from the Nikolic Defence team asked you about your gate duty. Your response was, and this is at page 10455 of the transcripts, quote: "Please do not ask me about dates because I do not remember dates."

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And no one is going to fault you, sir, or criticize you, but it's fair to say that you do not remember the specific dates of these events; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's also fair to say that with the passage of time, you've forgotten or are unclear about certain events that occurred during this very busy and stressful period of time within the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you testified here before, when I tried to find out from you whether you could tie your gate duty to the time that your fellow MPs were sent to Orahovac, your best recollection at that time was, and I quote: "Well, almost the entire Military Police Company was absent. Where they were, I really don't know. That's when I stayed at the gate, and that is why I stood at the gate in the first place because otherwise I never stood guard at the gate." And that was at page 10484. And I just want to review with you some other testimony that you gave, and then I'll put a question to you. Okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We just need an audible answer, that's all. Is that okay? I'm going to ask you a question in a moment. I'm just going read some testimony to you. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Trbic trial, you were asked about when your fellow MPs, including lawyers -- your fellow lawyers, Bogdanovic and Jovic, went to the field. This is page 33 of the transcript, and the question was put to you. Question: "So was it a common occurrence that either your two colleagues in your office would go and conduct field operations?" Your answer was: "No, it would not happen." Then the question was put to you: "So why were they in the field." And your answer was: "I truly do not know. This was decided by the Military Police Company commander." Then the follow-up question was put to you: "Well, you are on the gate. When did they leave? " Your answer was: "I truly do not know when they departed. I cannot recall the details. And at that point, actually, I was not even aware that they had left. I'm referring to the point in time when I was left at the gate." Then the next question that was put to you was: "And on that time, at that time, on that day you were on the gate, did you see any of the command staff leaving?" And your answer was: "I cannot recall precise names, but many officers came in and out of the barracks. It was quite crowded, so to say, but I cannot recall the names now, nor the faces, when it comes to all who are coming in and out." I'm just going to pause and let you catch up with the interpretation. I'm going to ask you some follow-up questions about that testimony, sir. So, when you testified in the Trbic case, you didn't know when in relation to assuming your duties at the gate your MP colleagues had gone into the field; right?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That is right, and I can repeat the same thing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, moreover, you testified in the Trbic trial that your gate duty could have lasted from 24 or even up to 48 hours, and that's at page 35 of the transcript in Sarajevo. So it's fair to say that you may have been at the gate for even more than 24 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It is possible. It is possible that I stayed there longer. I don't know if it was 25 or 26 hours. It may have been 23 for all I know. The only thing I know is that I was alone at the gate because there were no military policemen left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you testified in the Trbic case that it could have been 24 to 48 hours, is it possible that it was 36 hours, sir, that you were at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how much time I spent at the gate. It was a long time ago. I can't recall. I don't think it was as many as 36 hours. They returned before that. I don't think it was 36 hours. It's a long time; however, I'm not completely sure. I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you further testified, and again this is at page 35, and I quote: "While he was at the gate, I didn't even know where the Military Police Company was, where they were deployed, and so on." Do you stand by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were then asked: "Did you find out anything later on? Did you know when the -- when did these officers return to the barracks?" And you answered at page 36: "Soon after maybe; maybe after a day or two the company gathered; a day, two or three days. I don't know." And, sir, can you confirm that you were still unsure whether it was one, two, or possibly three days before the members of your MP company returned to Standard?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that. I truly don't know when they returned. They probably did not return all together the same time; they returned at different times. Someone may have returned after a day, others after two or three. All I know is that not all of them came in together at once, and that's what I am telling you now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just picking up on what you just said, sir, with respect to some of the MPs maybe returning at later times than others, did you ever become aware that some of the MPs were sent to more than one location during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So it's still your testimony, then, that to this day you don't know where your fellow MPs were sent over this one, two, or even three-day period; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time where they were. Now I do. I heard about that. However, while he was at the gate and around mid-July, I truly didn't know where the policemen had gone to. It wasn't up to me to decide where they would go, and I wasn't told where they went. After they returned, some of them told me where they were in the field. Now I know a bit more than then. I know where some of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, going back to this period in July of 1995, again just to pick up on what you just said, at the time when your fellow MP Company members were returning from the field, where did they tell you they had been assigned?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything and I wasn't asking. For example, the work mates that worked with me, they told me where they had been sent to, I didn't ask anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you just testified a couple of moments ago that "some of them told me where they were in the field," can you just tell the Trial Chamber who told you and what did they tell you about where they were in the field? Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, my work mates, Bogdanovic and some others, told me they were in Orahovac, in the field there. I know about them. I didn't ask anyone else about anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree that, as you sit here today, you don't know exactly which of those one, two, or three days when your colleagues were out in the field that you spent that period of time at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I was at the gate while there were no policemen in the barracks. As soon as they returned, those of them who were assigned to duty shifts at the gate took over. They were then at the gate, and I returned to my regular tasks. I don't know whether that was one, two, or three days after that. I truly can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you some questions, then, about your actual duty time at the gate. You testified earlier today that it started in the afternoon and that you were alone on that duty, and I take it you were alone the entire time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you ever left that post for any reason during the time you were serving at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps for brief periods of time, but I wasn't absent for any longer periods of time. Somebody always had to be at the gate, a military policemen had to be there. Perhaps I may have gone for a couple of minutes, but not longer than that, I'm certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. Jeremic. Is there a bathroom in that little reception area that you saw on the picture?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It I really don't know whether there was a toilet in the reception area. I don't think so. I think I had to go to the building, but it's only 15 or 20 metres away from the reception office, maybe a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Did someone bring you your meals, or, again, did you quickly run into the building to get your meals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I really don't remember how it went with my meals, whether I had lunch boxes or whether I had somebody bring it to me. I can't remember. However, I can repeat that I was not absent from the gate for any extended periods of time. I wasn't allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago when I read out that portion of your testimony in the Trbic trial, you referred to many officers coming in and out of the barracks and that it was, to use your words, "quite crowded, so to say" at this time when you were at the gate. As you sit here today, is it possible for you to remember the names of any of these officers who were coming and going?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: How? I don't understand when you say that it was quite crowded, that there were quite many military policemen? I was the only military policemen at Standard. Perhaps you meant just plain soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, sir. It may have been a translation issue, or I may have misspoken. I was citing to you your testimony from the Trbic trial where you testified about many officers, brigade officers, I believe, coming in and out of the barracks. We all understand that you were alone at the gate. So my question was: As you sit here today, is it possible for to you remember the names of any of those officers who were coming in and out?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you now. It was an emergency situation and people were brought back from their leave because they were needed. They were all present. Probably -- I really can't remember the name of an officer, whether he passed by. I really don't know. He may have, but I can't say with any certainty. I can't tell you I saw this or that person. I saw many people. I was at the gate, and I could see who was going in and out of Standard. As for anyone in particular, whether I saw them at this or that time, I truly can't say. I can tell you that there were quite many officers going in and out, perhaps all of the officers that were regularly at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Prosecution's position, sir, and there's been evidence before the Trial Chamber, is that Sretan Milosevic, Dragan Jokic, and Dragan Nikolic were on duty as duty operations officers during this period of time. Do you recall seeing any of them with that extra knowledge that I've giving you, suggesting to you that they were duty officers in the operations room during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague should make the period of duty that he is referring to more clear to the witness because there's three names, and they might be on duty for -- it's not for me to say how long they were on duty, but the question must be made clearer for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I actually anticipated what you were going to say. Yes, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this period of one, two, three days that we are talking about when your fellow MPs were in the field - and, sir, if you don't remember, that's okay. We are not going to fault you - I just want to know whether, as you sit here, you can recall for the Trial Chamber whether any of those individuals acted as duty operations officer during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may take a look at 65 ter 383, please, and we'll need to go to page 8 in the B/C/S and page 6 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm showing you, and I hope you can see it on your screen, is a page from the barracks duty officer book, not the operations duty officer book, but the book that was maintained by the so-called barracks duty officer. This was kept each day. Are you familiar with this document, sir, this book?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not familiar with this document. I was never the barracks duty officer; however, I know that there were duty officers for the barracks. Yes, I can recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down just a little bit in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is for the period of the 14th to the 15th of July 1995. And if we see at the bottom, do you see where it says: "A body of troops at the barracks was not counted due to the activities in the field; and, practically, only operations duty officer, duty officer, and guards were at the barracks." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, towards the bottom of the page. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, sir, that this reference to lack of officers, that doesn't sound like the day that you were at the gate, does it, because you saw, as you testified, a lot of officers coming in and out? Is that fair to say, that this doesn't sound like the day that you were at the gate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it would be better if the witness would remove his earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We want to know first whether he understands English. One moment. I want to know whether he understands English. Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Can you remove your headphones, please. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just before this gets too far, I mean, I understand this is cross-examination and that my colleague can suggest possibilities to the witness; however, he should not confuse him with a past answer that he gave. My colleague quoted from the transcript of the Sarajevo interview where when he mentioned that those officers were coming in and out is when the military police were leaving. Now he is referring to another document, and this other document is on the next day and not the day that the military police left. So at least he has to make those questions clear to the witness and not try to confuse him with the dates. The witness has already said that those dates are unknown to him. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this witness is capable of answering the question as it was put to him. I don't think there's any confusion going on. He has answered all the questions that I've asked him without hesitation. I'm simply asking him whether what he sees in this document is consistent with what he saw at the gate. If my friend has any other problems with that, he can try to clarify it on redirect. I don't see any reason to interrupt this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
