utterances.text: Okay. All we are interested in at the moment is to know whether the witness is capable of answering this question. If he is and you are not satisfied or you think there is a confusion, you can deal with it on redirect. Headphones back. Do you wish to repeat your question, Mr. Thayer? I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. I'll just put it to him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified quite clearly about seeing a lot of officers coming in and out of Standard at the time and being present at Standard at the time.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think you mentioned that you thought the people were being brought back at this period of time, which might explain why there were so many officers while you were at the gate. So my question is: Looking at this excerpt from the barracks log, where it refers to the only officers being present being the duty operations officer and the barracks duty officer, does it sound like this day is the day you were at the gate, or does it sound like this must be another day? That's all I'm asking you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain you. When I said that I saw many officers coming and going out of the barracks, I meant the officers who came to the barracks, took something, and went back. So there was a lot of coming and goings. I didn't say that I saw officers walking around the compound of the barracks. That is what I wanted to say, that's what I said the last time, and I'm saying it again. They came to fetch something. Whether they did or not, they stayed for a brief period of time and went out again. This is what I saw, that there was a lot of comings and goings. I didn't see them strolling around the compound. This is what I think I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you said in your testimony in the Trbic case -- I just want to make sure we understand you clearly. When you say it was "quite crowded, so to say," can you recall, as you sit here today, which officers; and if you can't remember names, that's fine. I'll adjust the question a little bit. Can you recall, can you give us any number of how many brigade officers actually were present at the brigade? Understanding that you've told us you saw a lot of officers coming and going, can you tell the Trial Chamber, can you give the Trial Chamber any idea of how many officers were present at Standard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to make a statement still make a statement, Mr. Bourgon, because I saw you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. He changed the question. "Present at Standard" is fine with me. It's a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly don't know. I can't give you any number. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of more questions for you, sir. In answer to a question from my friend earlier today, you testified that you don't recall whether there were VRS officers who were not members of the Zvornik Brigade coming in and out, but that it's possible. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P377 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a couple of pages from the duty operations officer notebook, sir, and we'll get there in just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are looking at page 131 of the document, please. 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in your own language there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's quite illegible. Well, yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment, one moment. We need to stop for just two minutes. Please stay here everyone. We'll be coming back soon. --- Break taken at 11.38 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hence forth, and until the end of this week, we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Kwon. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Do you see in the middle of the page, or slightly above the middle of the page, a phone number, 583-959, and an entry that says: "Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Zvornik Municipal Assembly, Zekic." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the time in July 1995, did you know who this person was, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I feel that was the president of the Executive Council, Zekic. Yes, I do know him. If we are talking about the same person, I think he was the president of the Executive Council, yes, of the Assembly. I knew who Zekic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we jump into private session for just one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back, yes. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it possible that during this time when you were at the gate, that this individual, Zekic, actually came to Standard for a meeting and you simply can't remember today because of the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, sir, it's possible that this meeting happened, that this individual was there, it's just that you don't remember because of the passage of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about this meeting. I don't remember. Yes, you are right. It was a long time ago and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's twice the same question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we go to page 143 of the English and the B/C/S, please -- sorry, page 133; not 143, 133. That's 133 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you? This is another page from the same duty operations officer notebook. There is a reference to Jokic and a delegation from Pilica. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it, but this is the first time I see it in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Do you know who Slavko Peric is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Slavko Peric? I don't know. Can you help me with providing -- with giving me some more details?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. Mr. Peric was the security officer for the 1st Battalion. Does that ring any bells for you? If it doesn't, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I knew quite a few security officers from the battalion, but I cannot remember a Peric. Probably, if I saw him, I would have remembered, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sir, there's been testimony in this case that Mr. Peric and some other members of his battalion arrived at Standard during this three-day period we are talking about, and that Mr. Peric was accompanied by some people who were in civilian clothes. Do you have any recollection of this individual and this delegation arriving?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I do. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, is it possible that they came and you just can't remember because of the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Anything is possible. If there had been a large group of civilians entering Standard during my shift, I would remember that, but I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you, you referred to Mr. Jekic and Mr. Vidovic. Mr. Jekic being a former high level MUP officer from Serbia, and Mr. Vidovic being the former chief of police of Mali Zvornik, would you consider those officers just regular civilians, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And they would have to show their share official credentials in order to be let through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: They certainly would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, my last question is: If during this period of time you were at the gate there was a small group of civilians, let's say two civilians, who came to Standard, isn't it possible that, number one, they came through for a short visit while you were not at your post?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I explained awhile ago that I was away just for brief periods of times. Maybe I was absent for a minute or two and I explained what the reasons for that were, but I would definitely not allow two strange civilians to come in so easily without checking their identity papers or without informing the duty operations officer about their identity, if, as you mentioned, those were two high ranking officers from the MUP of Serbia. But I don't -- I very much doubt that they would pass through unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer, you just said: "... if, as you mentioned, those were two high ranking officers from the MUP of Serbia." Do you mean to say that if they were such officers, it's possible that they came through? Is that what you were saying there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That's not what I wanted to say. You said two high ranking MUP officers and I just repeated your words. I didn't know whether they were officers or not; but if they were dressed in civilian clothes, they wouldn't have been able to pass through. I would stop them, check their ID papers, and ask for instructions from the duty operations officer because I didn't know who these people were. I don't know how they looked like. I had heard of them and I would find them interesting in a way, and that would definitely be something to help me memorize that these two appeared at my gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, again, sir, you would agree that it's possible that you've simply for gotten that, as you've have forgotten a lot of other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are being repetitive now. I mean, you put this question several times and this possibility several times, and you have had more than one answer. So let's move to your next question if you have any or else conclude here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is my final question. I thank you Mr. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there redirect, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a few questions for you, Mr. Jeremic. At page 34 lines 18 to 20, there was a question about what documents were shown to you by the Defence, and your answer was that we did not try to influence you in any way. But do you recall that we showed you those pictures that we used in Court today?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When we met this weekend here in The Hague, do you remember we showed you those pictures?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when you -- at page 35, lines 1 to 4, you mentioned in response to a question from my colleague that: "When we met, we spoke about Ratko Vidovic and Vojislav Jekic. "When I say "we," it is you and I, to be more precise. Did we ask you only about Ratko Vidovic and Vojislav Jekic, or did we also ask you about any civilians coming in on that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, we mostly discussed Jekic and Vidovic, but you did ask me how would I have reacted if any other civilians showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when my colleague quoted from your transcript before the Sarajevo court, he quoted the following passage, and that was at page 33, lines 20 to 22: "I cannot recall precise names, but many officers came in and out of the barracks. It was quite crowded, so to say, but I cannot recall the names now, nor the faces, when it comes to all those who were coming in and out." Does this comment apply to officers, and is the situation different for civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: There were no civilians whatsoever; I said that before. The situation was such that they were not in the vicinity of the barracks. They didn't even pass along the main road, and it was just the army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, one question I'd like to have for you: If you civilian or a person dressed in civilian clothes came in, in the same car as a brigade officer, is it possible that this person would be let through?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, if that person was in the company of a commander or a chief, I wouldn't stop such a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We have one question from the Bench. Judge Prost, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: You've covered this, I think, Mr. Jeremic to some degree, but I just wanted to be very clear here. At page 28 of the transcript today, lines 20 to 25, Mr. Bourgon put a question to you: "Would you let at any time an unknown civilian walk in the barracks without an escort." And the part of the answer I'm interested in is where you said: "Civilians were not allowed to enter the barracks, unknown civilians." I am wondering if there was a distinction, then, if a civilian happened to be known to the guards if he or she would be allowed to proceed into the barracks without an escort?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: If an officer was in civilian clothes, I would let him in without any checks. That's what I had in mind. Unfamiliar civilians would not be let in. If there was a civilian that I knew, for example, an officer in civilian clothes, I would let him pass through the gate. That's what I had in mind when I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you there are no further questions for you, which means that you are free to go. Staff will assist you. Thank you for coming again to give testimony; and, once more, we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good-bye to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bourgon, documents? You have got two photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, two pictures, 3DIC 222, which is a version of 3D500; and 3DIC 223, which is a picture of Exhibit 3D497. That's it, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are admitted. Do you have any documents, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That disposes of that witness. Let's go into private session for awhile before we go to the next witness, because I want to clarify something with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness, his name is not to be mentioned. Yes. We were informed that you will be seeking for the continuation of the protective measures granted to this person in another case continuation for this case. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. However, the e-mail that you sent to our senior legal officer seems to suggest that this person enjoyed in that trial, in those proceedings, the protective measures of pseudonym, face distortion, and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is the information we received during our meeting with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, I have been given the decision by that particular Trial Chamber which indicates that the protective measures granted to this individual were only of a pseudonym and face distortion. They did not include voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Defence is concerned, Your Honour, we have no problem with using the same measures as they applied in the last case. Perhaps the witness was wrong when he passed that information on. If you wish so, we can verify that once more with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision of the other Chamber goes back to August 2003, it's of the 26th, which you can check, I suppose. You would have a copy of it. So, have you verified? Have you been able to verify this, Mr. McCloskey in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We haven't, Mr. President, but we can just stay out of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we start with this witness. I think you need to bring down the curtains while he walks in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one further preliminary matter before we begin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- in public session, which also has to do with Witness 3DW-1, in terms of the scheduling of his testimony. Many suggestions were made yesterday that maybe he could begin today or maybe he could begin earlier on Thursday. It doesn't seem to be possible. Both options are not possible. Some people are not happy with the fact that he would begin an hour earlier, others -- other teams want to see the witness before he begins his testimony; therefore, we prefer to have him begin on Thursday. I did discuss the matter with the witness; and contrary to what I said yesterday, he has no obligations, he would have been able to begin earlier. But now he has checked his agenda and he is willing to stay until Monday, if that is necessary, to complete his testimony. So we can proceed as planned on Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a 92 ter witness, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's have it as brief as possible, then. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to start giving evidence as a witness for the Nikolic Defence team. You have testified here before, and when you did you were given two protective measures; namely, that of the use of a pseudonym instead of your real name and also the use of facial distortion. We have discussed this and we are going to keep them in place for the duration of your testimony in this trial now. Before you start giving evidence, you are required to make the solemn declaration you are familiar with. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the first part of your testimony, I think we will need to go into private session, so let's go into private session immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will address you as "Witness." Do you remember having given a statement to the Drago Nikolic Defence team on the 1st of June 2008?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read that statement yesterday during your proofing for the testimony here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the proceedings under Rule 92 ter, I wanted to read out the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mrs. Nikolic. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ratko Vidovic's police force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You start where I told you: "Based on his ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the beginning of the paragraph. Based on everything he knows and went through, the witness believes that Ratko Vidovic was deeply involved in the events in Zvornik in 1992. Ratko Vidovic's police unfoundedly arrested the witness in the territory of Serbia and turned him over to the people from Zvornik. The witness was then directly taken to the Alhos factory where he was abused. The witness believes that Ratko Vidovic cooperated with Arkan, SDS members, and other participants in the 1992 events. He carried out their orders and knew well what was taking place in Zvornik during that period. The witness did not know Vojo Jekic, but he heard that he was present in Zvornik during the events of 1992. The witness remembers Enver Abdic, who was the Zvornik Red Cross secretary, who was arrested in 1992, beaten, and killed. His body was found in 2007 during the exhumations carried out at Crni Vrh. Abdic's murder is linked to Jekic's activities in 19.92 in Zvornik. This concludes the reading of the summary pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have a few questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll have about a dozen questions, but I think this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a 25 minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this summary of the statement that I have read out, does that reflect your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are the facts contained in your statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: I believe they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do these facts fully reflect what you would have said for this Honourable Court had you been asked the same questions that you were asked in the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: I believe that what I said is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence the statement of Witness 3DW71; that is, document number 3D471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It will be under seal, of course. So let's proceed, and we'll give it a number later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a few more questions and I will curtail my redirect. On the day that you were arrested, at the place where you were arrested, did you talk to any of the policemen from Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but only after they put me into the car. Actually, I asked to talk to the police commander Vidovic. They contacted him and told him that he was at the petrol station in Mali Zvornik. They drove me there and that was in the direction of Bosnia -- or rather, Alhos, and they already had an order to hand me over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is the question. On that day, did you talk personally with Ratko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When they brought me to the petrol station, he was there, and I exchanged a few words with him. Actually, I asked him why I was arrested, if I was arrested at all, and why are they taking me to Bosnia to another republic, because at the time we still thought that we were one country. And the normal procedure would be to take an arrested person to the district court of that particular region, not to take them to another republic. He responded by saying that he could not help me, that I should go to Alhos and try to settle the issue there, which means that he must have had some orders from someone else to have me taken to Alhos without any additional questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know who he received the orders from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: I don't know directly, but I know who was present during my arrest and what this line of communication was. I was handed over directly to the president of the SDS, Brano Grujic, and Arkan's deputy, the "Major" or whatever he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know where Brano Grujic's whereabouts now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: I know that he is waiting in custody in Belgrade for trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like us to move into private session for the next few questions, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How long did you know Ratko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Well, certainly since the day I came to Zvornik until 1992. That would make it 20 years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a member of the commission that you just mentioned, did you learn about any activities of Ratko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: At that time, he and another colleague of his were accused of bringing vehicles from Austria and Germany illegally and selling them in Serbia and Bosnia. Due to that, he was suspended from the police. He left Zvornik after that, and the other colleague remained there and worked as a haulier. And after awhile, he turned up as a police officer in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Based on your 20 year long acquaintance with Ratko Vidovic, how would you describe him as a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: If we do not take into account what he did to me personally, and his responsibility for having me delivered to Alhos, although he knew what would happen to me, that I would be killed if I was detained there, I can say that he was a man who had committed an offence. And I also know that after the war he bought some business premises and a flat in Belgrade, and that was the time when people didn't have any food on their tables and were unable to satisfy their daily needs. I don't think that he could have afforded that on his civil servant's salary. So, regardless of all that, I would say that he was a dishonourable man for being responsible for what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During these meetings, did you hear of a man called Vojo Jekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Not initially; but sometime in March, his name mentioned came up. I cannot tell you exactly in what context, but I remember Brano Grujic saying several time that he had contact with Vojo. I didn't know what his position was, but I remember him being mentioned; although, names were rarely mentioned, but his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What about Predrag Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him personally in those days before the war. He was the secretary of the Zvornik municipality committee; and, later on, as a Bosnian-Herzegovinian caterer, he joined the State Security service in Belgrade. Some two weeks before the war, the both were mentioned in that context. I still don't know who they belonged to. I assumed that they were members of the same service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were these services involved in any activities at the beginning of war in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. We are getting so far into non-relevant, as far as I can see, materials. He has heard a guy's name, he doesn't know what context it's in, he heard he might be this, he heard he might be that. I don't know what good this is doing the Court. I think we've gotten out of the fact about the witness and this is not a 92 ter issue, and I just think there's just no probative value going here -- going down this line of inquiry with a witness, especially for this time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go into private session now, so that I can respond to this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, Ms. Nikolic, what you should be concerned with is that to provide us with enough information, enough testimony which would enable us to put the testimony of this gentleman and that of others, and that's it. I mean, because we are talking of events in 1992, and they are relevant only insofar as an allegation was made in the course of this testimony -- of this trial. So let's concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Would the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be no repetition of the question. There will be a new question that is beside the subject matter that you are trying to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is relative to the 1992 events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Enver Abdic personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW-017
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were friends. He was the secretary of the Red Cross of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Why do you think that Vojo Jekic had anything to do with the disappearance of Enver Abdic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection Mr. President. Where is this taking us in the long run. This kind of drive-by character assassination - perhaps this guys deserve it - but I don't think it does the Court any good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, what would be the relevance of this question, Ms. Nikolic? I don't think you understood what I told you before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, Your Honours, I will conclude my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No exam. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which basically means that we have finished here, unless Judge Prost and Judge Stole have any questions. Sir, we are finished with your testimony which means you can go back home. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Wait until the curtains are down because we must not show your face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, any documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The list has been submitted: The witness statement 473, and pseudonym sheet, 3D503 -- I apologise, the witness statement, 471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 471. All right. Okay. I take it there are no objections? So they are admitted under seal, both of them. Both documents will remain under seal, separately under seal. Is there anything else? One moment because while we are at this, I'll go back my notes. Okay. There was a Defence motion from the Borovcanin Defence team filed on the 11th of September, 2008, seeking leave to amend their 65 ter exhibit list with the documents indicated in the annex attached thereto. On the 17th of September -- this was filed on the 11th of September. On the 17th of September, following a prompt from the Bench, the Prosecution filed a response in which they did not object; therefore, here and now, we are granting this motion ordered. Then there was another motion from the same Defence team, the Borovcanin Defence team, for the admission of written evidence in lieu of oral testimony pursuant to 92 bis, together with an appendix. This was filed on the 15th of September. Basically, the Borovcanin team request the admission of a statement by one of the witnesses, Brigadier Grange, pursuant to rule 92 bis without requiring cross-examination. General Grange is a character witness. This was raised in Court on the 16th of September, and on that occasion, Mr. McCloskey, you said that you required some more time. A week has passed since then. I don't know whether you require more time or whether you are in a position to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've spoke within Mr. Gosnell and Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Thayer, and we have decided not to object to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there any objection from any of the other Defence teams? None. So that motion is also being, here and now, granted orally. Then there is the motion from General Miletic for authorisation to add some documents to the list of exhibits pursuant to rule 65 ter G. There is a confidential annex attached to it. This was filed on the 18th of September. As you will recall, we had put the question to the Prosecution on the 18th of September, the Prosecution said that it will be no problem; but the Gvero Defence team said that they were not ready at the time and would not be ready by Monday, 22nd of September. Today is the day after, the 23rd of September. Maybe Mr. Josse is in a position to enlighten us. If you require more time, we will, of course, accommodate you; but if you are in a position to tell us your position, we'll be glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since the Trial Chamber have kindly given us the option, we would rather have more time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next Monday, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That's that. Okay. So that's it. I don't think we have anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is reminding us that tomorrow there was a special request because of logistics that we do not start the videolink before 10 o'clock; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in that case, can I ask you if there is anything pending that you would like to deal with in open session or in private session tomorrow morning between 9.00 and 10.00, any other business that we could transact?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the moment. The Defence has no proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone else? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President. Without Mr. Bourgon here to discuss what we could argue about, I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That means if we can think of something ourselves, we will send you the message and we will start at 9.00; otherwise,we start at 10:00, or just before 10:00, to be ready for the videolink tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th of September, 2008, at 10.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
